name: Beth Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What does your usual day on the lines involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am an experienced lineworker with an electricity company, building or repairing power lines as the orders come in. My certificate and apprenticeship gave me the habits: check the site, isolate the line, then do the work with the crew. I am fifty-eight and still happy to take a repair day, though the long storm nights are harder than they once were. My partner and I have grown children, and we have talked about stopping full-time work around sixty-six if the income figures make sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say an AI plateau means the depot gets a few faster forms and my crew still repairs the line. I sometimes use an AI tool to check a draft note, then ask the crew to verify the job number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My typical pay and several months of savings make the next few years feel steady if shifts continue. I have an idea of finishing full-time line work around sixty-six, but I have not treated that as a guaranteed date. A power line repair is not finished because an AI note found a neat ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my usual repair rota and compare drafted notes with signed work sheets. In the first year I would request an updated retirement income estimate and set it beside our ordinary monthly costs before changing our plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about this picture. There is enough work in it for me to keep earning while we check the retirement figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a draft note unsafe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A note could close a repair before the second inspection is signed. I would check both signatures on the work sheet before marking the line complete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the retirement estimate is lower than you expected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would adjust the target date after looking at our actual spending. We have some savings, but I would not promise to stop at sixty-six without enough income.

say: **AI** may speed depot notes while the crew still repairs and signs each power line job.
I would **keep** full-time work while checking retirement income.
think: **Typical** pay and several months saved make steady shifts reassuring.
**Stopping** around sixty-six is a personal target, subject to actual income and costs.
do: **Keep** repair rota and check AI drafted notes against signed work sheets.
**Request** updated retirement income estimate and compare it with monthly costs.
feel: **Calm** about work while keeping retirement plans conditional.
S0.quote: A power line repair is not finished because an AI note found a neat ending.
fieldNote: She **uses** AI occasionally but relies on signed inspections.
The **retirement** target is personal and conditional on income covering ordinary household costs; no payment amount or statutory age is presumed.

steps.text: Keep repair shifts and compare drafted notes with signed work sheets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that AI might make booking and buying quicker, but it should not erase travel or isolation time from the job sheet. I would let a younger crew member try the new scheduling view and show me where it gets the day wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking work in the office changes ahead of my hands-on repairs. Still, if they trim callout hours, our plan to finish full-time work around sixty-six could move, and I do not want to guess that from a sales slide. A shorter AI callout entry does not shorten the ladder or the power line isolation check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the supervisor for six weeks of old and new callout schedules side by side. In the first year I would log any lost paid hours, and if the reduction lasts three months I would add eighty from each remaining pay packet to our retirement savings if our household budget allows it, while we review the finish date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible lost hours, but there is time to see actual hours. I am willing to change a routine after someone proves the new one works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the two schedules tell you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the paid hours, travel time and isolation time for the same kind of job. A shorter calendar entry is not proof the crew worked fewer minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if hours do not fall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the current retirement target and normal spending. I would not start the extra transfer unless the paid-hour reduction lasts long enough to be real.

say: **Booking** AI may help, but schedules must count travel and isolation.
I would **compare** old and new paid hours before changing my retirement plan.
think: **Office** work changes first, while a callout reduction could affect my later income.
The **target** of finishing around sixty-six stays provisional until paid hours are known.
do: **Compare** old and new callout schedules for six weeks.
**Log** paid-hour changes during the first year.
**Add** eighty from each remaining pay packet to savings only after three months of reduced hours, if affordable.
feel: **Anxious** about possible hour cuts, though able to check the evidence.
S1.quote: A shorter AI callout entry does not shorten the ladder or the power line isolation check.
fieldNote: She **accepts** scheduling changes only after a measured comparison with actual work.
The **extra** savings transfer is conditional on three months of lower paid hours.

steps.text: Compare six weeks of new and old callout schedules
Save eighty extra from each remaining pay packet after three months of reduced hours if affordable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI by 2028 changes dispatch at sixty, and capable line robots around 2031 could arrive when I am sixty-three. I would insist on a proper field trial before a robot takes a repair callout from a crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I had hoped to keep earning until around sixty-six, subject to the figures. If a robot cuts my hours at sixty-three, several months of savings will not fill three years of missing pay, even though some lineworker jobs are nearby. Three months of savings will not stretch across three years of missing lineworker wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would request two retirement income estimates, one for finishing at sixty-three and one at sixty-six. In the first year after 2028 I would compare those estimates with household costs; if the earlier figure covers us and callout hours fall, I would bring my full-time finish forward to sixty-three instead of chasing uncertain shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because the robot date sits inside my own working plan. I can compare the sums, but I cannot make three years of wage gap disappear by being positive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the sixty-three income estimate does not cover costs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking safe repair shifts and ask the supervisor what other paid field work exists. I would not retire early merely because the robot is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change towns for another lineworker job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare any written nearby offer first. My partner and our grown children are here, so a move would need far more than a vacancy advertisement.

say: **Robots** around 2031 could affect repairs when I am sixty-three.
I would **require** proper field trials before robots take paid callouts.
think: **Several** months of savings cannot replace three years of wages before my provisional sixty-six finish.
**Some** nearby jobs give options, but an earlier retirement needs adequate income.
do: **Request** written income estimates for stopping at sixty-three and sixty-six.
**Compare** each estimate with household costs after 2028.
**Bring** full-time retirement to sixty-three only if income covers costs and callouts fall.
feel: **Anxious** about a pay gap inside my expected working years.
S2.quote: Three months of savings will not stretch across three years of missing lineworker wages.
fieldNote: Her **personal** target makes the 2031 robot date material without assuming a statutory pension age.
**Early** retirement is an actual conditional change from her own sixty-six plan.

steps.text: Bring retirement forward to sixty-three if income covers costs and callouts fall
Keep safe line repair shifts if earlier income is inadequate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that full thinking AI by 2031 reaches the depot at sixty-three for me, and capable robots around 2034 arrive when I am sixty-six. I would want paid workers alongside robots on those first repair jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That robot date is close to the age I had pencilled in to finish full-time work. If our actual retirement income covers costs, I can stay with the crew until then, but a weak estimate could keep me needing shifts after sixty-six. A line robot turning up when I am sixty-six is easier to face if the retirement figures actually cover breakfast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request an updated retirement estimate this year and review it with my partner each year. If the amount by sixty-six covers our costs, I would keep line shifts through 2031 and finish full-time work around 2034; if it does not, I would ask about paid ground inspection duties rather than assume I can climb indefinitely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, though not pressed into an early exit. Five years lets me check whether the number and the job still meet in the same place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would ground inspection involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check materials and completed repair records at the site, with someone qualified still doing the climb. I would need a written paid assignment before counting on that income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your partner wants you to stop storm nights sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would put the actual income estimate next to our bills before changing the date. I can take fewer nights only if the household can carry it.

say: The **robot** date around 2034 is near my tentative full-time finish at sixty-six.
**Paid** workers should stay alongside early line robots.
think: **Adequate** retirement income could let me stay on the line until my planned finish.
An **insufficient** estimate would make paid ground work more important than a calendar date.
do: **Review** retirement income estimate with partner each year.
**Keep** line shifts through 2031 if safe and income remains needed.
**Seek** written paid ground inspection duty if sixty-six retirement income falls short.
feel: **Uneasy** about the figures but free of a forced early decision.
S3.quote: A line robot turning up when I am sixty-six is easier to face if the retirement figures actually cover breakfast.
fieldNote: She **compares** a possible retirement date with household costs, not an assumed legal entitlement.
**Ground** inspection is conditional on a written paid assignment if retirement income falls short.

steps.text: Keep line shifts through 2031 while work remains safe
Seek paid ground inspection duty if age-sixty-six income falls short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI in 2036 and capable robots around 2039 would come after the age I hope to leave full-time line work. The company should still teach younger lineworkers to inspect a fault rather than trust a machine’s neat plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-eight at thinking AI and seventy-one at robots, so I might already be away from the crew if our income checks out at sixty-six. I cannot promise that today; several months of savings alone do not fund a long retirement. A robot may climb a power line after I leave, but an apprentice still needs to know why the test matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking repair shifts now and request a fresh retirement estimate each year. If the age-sixty-six figure covers our costs, I would follow our existing plan to finish full-time work then; if it does not, I would continue safe paid work and ask about part-time site checking when it is actually offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the technology arriving later, although the retirement arithmetic still needs doing. My plan is a set of numbers we can revise, not a date printed on a birthday card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss if you left the crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would miss the moment a repair brings a street back, and I would miss the younger workers asking why a test matters. I would not miss the long storm nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take unpaid mentoring after leaving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might visit a training day, but I would not build our household budget on unpaid work. Any regular site checking would need an actual paid offer.

say: A **decade** places capable robots after my provisional full-time finish.
**Apprentices** still need physical fault checks whatever the machine can do.
think: I **may** be away from line work by sixty-eight if actual retirement income is enough.
**Several** months of savings alone cannot guarantee a long retirement.
do: **Keep** repair shifts and request a retirement estimate each year.
**Follow** existing age-sixty-six finish only if income covers costs.
**Continue** safe paid work or seek offered part-time site checking if income falls short.
feel: **Calm** about later AI, while still checking retirement arithmetic.
S4.quote: A robot may climb a power line after I leave, but an apprentice still needs to know why the test matters.
fieldNote: Her **longer** timeline separates AI risk from the unresolved personal question of retirement income.
The **age-sixty-six** finish is an existing conditional plan, not newly accelerated retirement.

steps.text: Keep line shifts and update retirement estimates annually
Leave full-time line work at planned age-sixty-six if income covers costs
Seek paid part-time site checking if retirement income falls short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots around 2031 could cut my lineworker hours at sixty-three, three years before I hope to finish full-time work. A written retirement income comparison and paid field work if the early number is too small would help. The ladder does not care that my retirement plan was pencilled in for sixty-six.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how many older workers would still be climbing because the sums do not add up. I know the work and I can learn a proven tool, but I need an honest pay figure for any ground job. An offer on paper matters more than talk of a gentle transition.

headlineQuote: The ladder does not care that my retirement plan was pencilled in for sixty-six.
portrait: **Beth** is a fifty-eight-year-old electricity company lineworker whose certificate and apprenticeship taught her careful isolation and repair checks.
**Typical** pay and one to six months of savings support her and her partner, with grown children and retirement in sight.
She **occasionally** uses AI for notes and will test proven scheduling changes against actual paid hours.
She **hopes** to finish full-time work around sixty-six if income permits; the 2031 robot date could prompt an earlier conditional exit.
biggestWorry: **AGI** by 2028 could bring line robots around 2031 when she is sixty-three, before her provisional sixty-six finish.
whatWouldHelp: **Written** retirement income comparisons and actual paid field options would help if early retirement cannot cover household costs.
